claim: Neuropeptides are evolutionarily ancient peptide hormones of the nervous and neuroendocrine systems.
source: Neuropeptides are evolutionarily ancient peptide hormones of the nervous and neuroendocrine systems, and are thought to have regulated metamorphosis in early animal ancestors.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract and introduction, drawing from scientific consensus.

claim: Neuropeptides are thought to have regulated metamorphosis in early animal ancestors.
source: Neuropeptides are evolutionarily ancient peptide hormones of the nervous and neuroendocrine systems, and are thought to have regulated metamorphosis in early animal ancestors.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about ancestral function based on comparative evidence.

claim: The Wamide family of neuropeptides is shared across Bilateria and Cnidaria.
source: In particular, the deeply conserved Wamide family of neuropeptides—shared across Bilateria (e.g. insects and worms) and its sister group Cnidaria (e.g. jellyfishes and corals)—has been implicated in mediating life-cycle transitions, yet their endogenous roles remain poorly understood.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge based on comparative genomics and phylogenetic relationships.

claim: Wamide neuropeptides have been implicated in mediating life-cycle transitions.
source: In particular, the deeply conserved Wamide family of neuropeptides—shared across Bilateria (e.g. insects and worms) and its sister group Cnidaria (e.g. jellyfishes and corals)—has been implicated in mediating life-cycle transitions, yet their endogenous roles remain poorly understood.
evidence: This is based on prior research cited throughout the manuscript.

claim: The endogenous roles of Wamide neuropeptides remain poorly understood.
source: In particular, the deeply conserved Wamide family of neuropeptides—shared across Bilateria (e.g. insects and worms) and its sister group Cnidaria (e.g. jellyfishes and corals)—has been implicated in mediating life-cycle transitions, yet their endogenous roles remain poorly understood.
evidence: This is an assessment of the state of knowledge in the field, providing rationale for the study.

claim: GLWamide regulates the timing of life cycle transition in Nematostella vectensis.
source: By using CRISPR-Cas9-mediated reverse genetics, we show that cnidarian Wamide—referred to as GLWamide—regulates the timing of life cycle transition in the sea anemone cnidarian Nematostella vectensis.
evidence: This is the main finding supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Mutant planula larvae lacking GLWamides transform into morphologically normal polyps at a rate slower than wildtype control larvae.
source: We find that mutant planula larvae lacking GLWamides transform into morphologically normal polyps at a rate slower than that of the wildtype control larvae.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing knockout mutants to wildtype controls.

claim: Treatment of GLWamide null mutant larvae with synthetic GLWamide peptides is sufficient to restore a normal rate of metamorphosis.
source: Treatment of GLWamide null mutant larvae with synthetic GLWamide peptides is sufficient to restore a normal rate of metamorphosis.
evidence: This is supported by rescue experiments with synthetic peptides.

claim: GLWamide plays a dispensable, modulatory role in accelerating metamorphosis in Nematostella vectensis.
source: These results demonstrate that GLWamide plays a dispensable, modulatory role in accelerating metamorphosis in a sea anemone.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing delayed but not blocked metamorphosis.

claim: Neuropeptides are expressed in many cells of the nervous and neuroendocrine systems of Bilateria and Cnidaria.
source: Neuropeptides are evolutionarily ancient hormones—secreted, diffusible signaling-molecules—that are expressed in many cells of the nervous and neuroendocrine systems of Bilateria (e.g. vertebrates, insects and worms) and its sister group Cnidaria (e.g. jellyfishes, corals and sea anemones) (Grimmelikhuijzen and Hauser, 2012; Grimmelikhuijzen et al., 2002; Hartenstein, 2006; Walker et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Neuropeptides are short polypeptides generated from larger precursor proteins through proteolytic cleavage.
source: They are short polypeptides generated from larger precursor proteins through proteolytic cleavage, and are stored in membrane-bound secretory vesicles that are distributed throughout the neuron.
evidence: This is established knowledge about neuropeptide biochemistry.

claim: Neuropeptides are stored in membrane-bound secretory vesicles that are distributed throughout the neuron.
source: They are short polypeptides generated from larger precursor proteins through proteolytic cleavage, and are stored in membrane-bound secretory vesicles that are distributed throughout the neuron.
evidence: This is established knowledge about neuropeptide cell biology.

claim: Peptide α-amidation occurs via a post-translational, enzymatic conversion of a C-terminal glycine into an amide group.
source: For some, peptide α-amidation occurs via a post-translational, enzymatic conversion of a C-terminal glycine into an amide group, and is often critical for biological activity (reviewed in [Eipper et al., 1992]).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: Peptide α-amidation is often critical for biological activity of neuropeptides.
source: For some, peptide α-amidation occurs via a post-translational, enzymatic conversion of a C-terminal glycine into an amide group, and is often critical for biological activity (reviewed in [Eipper et al., 1992]).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: Intercellular signaling occurs when neuropeptides are released from secretory vesicles into the extracellular space and received by receptors of target cells.
source: Intercellular signaling occurs when neuropeptides are released from the secretory vesicles into the extracellular space and received by receptors of target cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about neuropeptide signaling mechanisms.

claim: Neuropeptides have been implicated in regulating behavior, physiology, and development in animals with nervous systems.
source: Neuropeptides have been implicated in regulating a wide range of biological processes—from behavior, physiology, and development—in animals with nervous systems (summarized in [Strand, 1999]).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a summary article.

claim: Neuropeptides were early neurotransmitters in the evolution of nervous systems.
source: Given that neuropeptides were early neurotransmitters in the evolution of nervous systems, testing hypotheses about the conserved roles of neuropeptides in extant animals is directly relevant to understanding how the primitive nervous system may have functioned.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about nervous system evolution.

claim: Several peptide hormones are shared across Bilateria and Cnidaria, including insulin-related peptide, glycoprotein hormone, prokineticin, and amidated peptides with carboxy-terminal sequences Wamide, RFamide and RYamide.
source: Comparative genomic evidence suggests that several peptide hormones are shared across Bilateria and Cnidaria, namely an insulin-related peptide, glycoprotein hormone, prokineticin, and amidated peptides with carboxy-terminal sequences Wamide, RFamide and RYamide (Jékely, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by comparative genomic evidence cited in the text.

claim: Only amidated peptides have been shown to occur in neurons of both bilaterians and cnidarians.
source: Among them, only amidated peptides have been shown to occur in neurons of both bilaterians and cnidarians (e.g. (Conzelmann and Jékely, 2012; Conzelmann et al., 2013; Grimmelikhuijzen, 1985; Koizumi et al., 2004; Schmich et al., 1998a); see also (Walker et al., 2009) for a review of literature on RFamide), and thus are here considered bona fide conserved neuropeptides.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Amidated peptides are considered bona fide conserved neuropeptides.
source: Among them, only amidated peptides have been shown to occur in neurons of both bilaterians and cnidarians (e.g. (Conzelmann and Jékely, 2012; Conzelmann et al., 2013; Grimmelikhuijzen, 1985; Koizumi et al., 2004; Schmich et al., 1998a); see also (Walker et al., 2009) for a review of literature on RFamide), and thus are here considered bona fide conserved neuropeptides.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited evidence of neuronal expression in both groups.

claim: The precursor protein of conserved neuropeptides typically encodes multiple copies of immature neuropeptides.
source: The precursor protein of these neuropeptides typically encodes multiple copies of immature neuropeptides (e.g. (Conzelmann and Jékely, 2012; Darmer et al., 1991; Leviev and Grimmelikhuijzen, 1995), some of which can differ in amino acid sequence; this indicates that an immature neuropeptide sequence can duplicate and diverge within a gene.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research on neuropeptide precursor structure.

claim: Immature neuropeptide sequences encoded by precursor proteins can differ in amino acid sequence.
source: The precursor protein of these neuropeptides typically encodes multiple copies of immature neuropeptides (e.g. (Conzelmann and Jékely, 2012; Darmer et al., 1991; Leviev and Grimmelikhuijzen, 1995), some of which can differ in amino acid sequence; this indicates that an immature neuropeptide sequence can duplicate and diverge within a gene.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: An immature neuropeptide sequence can duplicate and diverge within a gene.
source: The precursor protein of these neuropeptides typically encodes multiple copies of immature neuropeptides (e.g. (Conzelmann and Jékely, 2012; Darmer et al., 1991; Leviev and Grimmelikhuijzen, 1995), some of which can differ in amino acid sequence; this indicates that an immature neuropeptide sequence can duplicate and diverge within a gene.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of multiple, divergent copies within precursor proteins.

claim: Paralogous neuropeptides can be generated from a single gene or from different genes that emerged by gene duplication.
source: Paralogous neuropeptides can thus be generated from a single gene, or from different genes that emerged by gene duplication (i.e. paralogous genes).
evidence: This is an inference about evolutionary mechanisms based on the structure of neuropeptide genes.

claim: Neuropeptides can be lost during evolution.
source: Neuropeptides can also be lost during evolution; for example, deuterostome bilaterians (e.g. chordates and echinoderms) lack Wamide precursor orthologs (Conzelmann et al., 2013), and the RYamide-encoding gene appears absent from the genome of anthozoan cnidarians (sea anemones and corals; e.g. (Anctil, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations showing absence of specific neuropeptides in certain lineages.

claim: Deuterostome bilaterians lack Wamide precursor orthologs.
source: Neuropeptides can also be lost during evolution; for example, deuterostome bilaterians (e.g. chordates and echinoderms) lack Wamide precursor orthologs (Conzelmann et al., 2013), and the RYamide-encoding gene appears absent from the genome of anthozoan cnidarians (sea anemones and corals; e.g. (Anctil, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to comparative genomic research.

claim: The RYamide-encoding gene appears absent from the genome of anthozoan cnidarians.
source: Neuropeptides can also be lost during evolution; for example, deuterostome bilaterians (e.g. chordates and echinoderms) lack Wamide precursor orthologs (Conzelmann et al., 2013), and the RYamide-encoding gene appears absent from the genome of anthozoan cnidarians (sea anemones and corals; e.g. (Anctil, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to genomic analysis.

claim: Wamide is expressed in larval nervous systems in bilaterians.
source: First, Wamide is expressed in larval nervous systems in bilaterians (e.g. (Conzelmann et al., 2013; Hua et al., 1999) and cnidarians (e.g. [Leitz and Lay, 1995]).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Wamide is expressed in larval nervous systems in cnidarians.
source: First, Wamide is expressed in larval nervous systems in bilaterians (e.g. (Conzelmann et al., 2013; Hua et al., 1999) and cnidarians (e.g. [Leitz and Lay, 1995]).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Exogenous Wamides have effects on molecular, behavioral and/or morphogenetic processes underlying life cycle transition across animals.
source: Second, exogenous Wamides have effects on molecular, behavioral and/or morphogenetic processes underlying life cycle transition across animals.
evidence: This is supported by multiple examples cited in the following sentences.

claim: Wamide neuropeptides can inhibit the synthesis of juvenile hormone in crickets.
source: For instance, Wamide neuropeptides (also known as allatostatin-B, prothoracicostatic peptides, myoinhibitory peptides (MIP), and GLWamide) can inhibit the synthesis of juvenile hormone in crickets (Lorenz et al., 1995) and that of ecdysteroids (the molting hormone) in a silkworm (Hua et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Wamide neuropeptides can inhibit the synthesis of ecdysteroids in a silkworm.
source: For instance, Wamide neuropeptides (also known as allatostatin-B, prothoracicostatic peptides, myoinhibitory peptides (MIP), and GLWamide) can inhibit the synthesis of juvenile hormone in crickets (Lorenz et al., 1995) and that of ecdysteroids (the molting hormone) in a silkworm (Hua et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Wamide neuropeptides can induce larval settlement of trochophore larvae in annelids.
source: Also, they can induce larval settlement of trochophore larvae in annelids (Conzelmann et al., 2013), and metamorphosis of planula larvae into polyps in hydrozoan and scleractinian (hard coral) cnidarians (Erwin and Szmant, 2010; Iwao et al., 2002; Leitz et al., 1994; Schmich et al., 1998b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Wamide neuropeptides can induce metamorphosis of planula larvae into polyps in hydrozoan and scleractinian cnidarians.
source: Also, they can induce larval settlement of trochophore larvae in annelids (Conzelmann et al., 2013), and metamorphosis of planula larvae into polyps in hydrozoan and scleractinian (hard coral) cnidarians (Erwin and Szmant, 2010; Iwao et al., 2002; Leitz et al., 1994; Schmich et al., 1998b).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Wamide signaling appears to be necessary for life cycle transition across Bilateria and Cnidaria.
source: Third, Wamide signaling appears to be necessary for life cycle transition across Bilateria and Cnidaria.
evidence: This is based on evidence from knockdown experiments cited in the following sentences.

claim: Morpholino-mediated knockdown of MIP receptor expression blocked MIP-induced larval settlement behavior in Platynereis dumerilii.
source: The evidence comes from the annelid bilaterian Platynereis dumerilii, where morpholino-mediated knockdown of MIP receptor expression blocked MIP-induced larval settlement behavior (Conzelmann et al., 2013); but see Discussion), and the hydrozoan cnidarian Hydractinia echinate, where RNAi-mediated knockdown of GLWamide precursor expression can decrease rates of metamorphosis, and synthetic GLWamide could rescue metamorphosis-less phenotype that resulted from pharmacological inhibition of neuropeptide amidation (Plickert et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: RNAi-mediated knockdown of GLWamide precursor expression can decrease rates of metamorphosis in Hydractinia echinate.
source: The evidence comes from the annelid bilaterian Platynereis dumerilii, where morpholino-mediated knockdown of MIP receptor expression blocked MIP-induced larval settlement behavior (Conzelmann et al., 2013); but see Discussion), and the hydrozoan cnidarian Hydractinia echinate, where RNAi-mediated knockdown of GLWamide precursor expression can decrease rates of metamorphosis, and synthetic GLWamide could rescue metamorphosis-less phenotype that resulted from pharmacological inhibition of neuropeptide amidation (Plickert et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Synthetic GLWamide could rescue metamorphosis-less phenotype that resulted from pharmacological inhibition of neuropeptide amidation in Hydractinia echinate.
source: The evidence comes from the annelid bilaterian Platynereis dumerilii, where morpholino-mediated knockdown of MIP receptor expression blocked MIP-induced larval settlement behavior (Conzelmann et al., 2013); but see Discussion), and the hydrozoan cnidarian Hydractinia echinate, where RNAi-mediated knockdown of GLWamide precursor expression can decrease rates of metamorphosis, and synthetic GLWamide could rescue metamorphosis-less phenotype that resulted from pharmacological inhibition of neuropeptide amidation (Plickert et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Reduced rates of metamorphosis in GLWamide-deficient hydrozoan larvae were not consistently observed across independent experiments despite a near-complete loss of endogenous GLWamide precursor transcripts.
source: However, reduced rates of metamorphosis in GLWamide-deficient hydrozoan larvae were not consistently observed across independent experiments despite a near-complete loss of endogenous GLWamide precursor transcripts.
evidence: This is an observation from prior research that motivates the current study.

claim: It was proposed that quantitatively small amounts of GLWamide might be sufficient for larvae to remain competent to metamorphosis induction.
source: It was therefore proposed that quantitatively small amounts of GLWamide might be sufficient for larvae to remain competent to metamorphosis induction.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed to explain inconsistent results in prior research.

claim: The genome of Nematostella vectensis encodes one Wamide (GLWamide) precursor homolog (Nv126270).
source: The genome of the sea anemone Nematostella vectensis (Putnam et al., 2007) encodes one Wamide (GLWamide, MH939200) precursor homolog (Nv126270) (Anctil, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by genomic data and citations.

claim: The GLWamide precursor gene was predicted to contain a single exon based on in silico gene prediction.
source: The GLWamide precursor gene was predicted to contain a single exon based on in silico gene prediction (http://genome.jgi.doe.gov/cgi-bin/dispGeneModel?db=Nemve1&id=126270); however, comparison of the N. vectensis genome and cDNA sequences instead shows that the GLWamide gene consists of two exons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on computational gene prediction.

claim: Comparison of the N. vectensis genome and cDNA sequences shows that the GLWamide gene consists of two exons.
source: The GLWamide precursor gene was predicted to contain a single exon based on in silico gene prediction (http://genome.jgi.doe.gov/cgi-bin/dispGeneModel?db=Nemve1&id=126270); however, comparison of the N. vectensis genome and cDNA sequences instead shows that the GLWamide gene consists of two exons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing genome and cDNA sequences, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The GLWamide gene encodes different copy numbers of nine distinct GLWamide peptides that vary in N-terminal sequence.
source: The analysis of putative endoproteolytic cleavage sites (i.e. acidic and basic amino acid residues; (Darmer et al., 1991; Leviev and Grimmelikhuijzen, 1995) and C-terminal amidation sites (i.e. C-terminal Gly residue) in the predicted precursor protein sequence suggests that the GLWamide gene encodes different copy numbers of nine distinct GLWamide peptides that vary in N-terminal sequence (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis of the precursor protein sequence, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: NvLWamide-like gene (Nv242283) is predicted to generate and release QCPPGLWGC peptides, but not GLWamides, because of the lack of the canonical amidation signal, glycine, at the C-terminus.
source: We note that previously documented NvLWamide-like gene (Nv242283; (Havrilak et al., 2017) is predicted to generate and release QCPPGLWGC peptides, but not GLWamides, because of the lack of the canonical amidation signal, glycine, at the C-terminus (see Figure 5—figure supplement 1 for experimental validation).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and experimental validation shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: GLWamide precursor transcripts were first detected in ectodermal sensory cells in the outer epithelium and in the pharynx during early-mid planula development.
source: Consistent with previously published gene/peptide expression data (Nakanishi et al., 2012; Watanabe et al., 2014), GLWamide precursor transcripts were first detected in ectodermal sensory cells in the outer epithelium and in the pharynx during early-mid planula development (arrowheads in Figure 1A,B; inset in A) when a bundle of long cilia known as the apical tuft develops at the aboral pole.
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1A,B and consistent with prior publications.

claim: GLWamide transcripts appear in a subset of endodermal epithelial cells in the body column at the mid-planula stage.
source: At the mid-planula stage, GLWamide transcripts appear in a subset of endodermal epithelial cells in the body column (arrowheads in Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: GLWamide-positive sensory cells in the pharynx were often asymmetrically distributed along the directive axis.
source: Interestingly, GLWamide-positive sensory cells in the pharynx were often asymmetrically distributed along the directive axis, oriented perpendicular to the oral-aboral axis (inset in Figure 1D; [Watanabe et al., 2014]).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1D inset and consistent with prior publication.

claim: GLWamide peptide expression is detected in neuronal processes of the ectodermal and endodermal nervous systems at the mid-late planula stage.
source: Immunostaining revealed GLWamide peptide expression in a number of neuronal processes of the ectodermal and endodermal nervous systems at the mid-late planula stage (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: Ectodermal sensory cells of the body column extend basal processes aborally or laterally, but not toward the oral direction.
source: Ectodermal sensory cells of the body column extend basal processes aborally or laterally, but not toward the oral direction (Figure 2C,D), while GLWamide-positive pharyngeal sensory cells extend neurites in any direction (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: GLWamide-positive pharyngeal sensory cells extend neurites in any direction.
source: Ectodermal sensory cells of the body column extend basal processes aborally or laterally, but not toward the oral direction (Figure 2C,D), while GLWamide-positive pharyngeal sensory cells extend neurites in any direction (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2E,F.

claim: In the endoderm, GLWamide expression is detected in neurons that form longitudinal neurite bundles.
source: In the endoderm, GLWamide expression is detected in neurons that form longitudinal neurite bundles (Figure 2G,H).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2G,H.

claim: Prior to transformation into a polyp, GLWamides are expressed in neurons and their neurites that constitute ectodermal and endodermal neural networks of the planula larva.
source: These results demonstrate that, prior to transformation into a polyp through formation of oral tentacles, GLWamides are expressed in neurons and their neurites that constitute ectodermal and endodermal neural networks of the planula larva.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the expression data presented in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: CRISPR-Cas9-mediated mutagenesis can create null mutant alleles by introducing frameshift-causing indel mutations in the 5' region of the gene via an error-prone, non-homologous end-joining (NHEJ) DNA repair mechanism.
source: This approach can create null mutant alleles at the target gene locus in two ways: (1) by introducing frameshift-causing indel mutations in the 5' region of the gene via an error-prone, non-homologous end-joining (NHEJ) DNA repair mechanism, so that the translated peptide sequence is altered, and (2) by deleting the protein-coding region of the gene upon cleavages at flanking sites (cf. [Nakayama et al., 2013]).
evidence: This is established knowledge about CRISPR-Cas9 mechanisms, supported by a citation.

claim: CRISPR-Cas9-mediated mutagenesis can create null mutant alleles by deleting the protein-coding region of the gene upon cleavages at flanking sites.
source: This approach can create null mutant alleles at the target gene locus in two ways: (1) by introducing frameshift-causing indel mutations in the 5' region of the gene via an error-prone, non-homologous end-joining (NHEJ) DNA repair mechanism, so that the translated peptide sequence is altered, and (2) by deleting the protein-coding region of the gene upon cleavages at flanking sites (cf. [Nakayama et al., 2013]).
evidence: This is established knowledge about CRISPR-Cas9 mechanisms, supported by a citation.

claim: Injected F0 animals were usually mosaic mutants.
source: However, injected animals--here referred to as 'F0' animals--were usually mosaic mutants (Figure 3—figure supplement 1; [Servetnick et al., 2017]); mutagenesis occurred mosaically in an F0 embryo so that individual cells would carry different mutations, or no mutation at all.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and a citation.

claim: Mutagenesis occurred mosaically in an F0 embryo so that individual cells would carry different mutations, or no mutation at all.
source: However, injected animals--here referred to as 'F0' animals--were usually mosaic mutants (Figure 3—figure supplement 1; [Servetnick et al., 2017]); mutagenesis occurred mosaically in an F0 embryo so that individual cells would carry different mutations, or no mutation at all.
evidence: This is an explanation of the mosaic nature of F0 mutants, supported by data and citation.

claim: Three different null mutant alleles at the GLWamide locus (glw-a, glw-b, and glw-c) were found, all of which carried frameshift mutations predicted to inhibit normal translation of neuropeptide precursor sequences.
source: Upon screening, we found three different null mutant alleles at the GLWamide locus (glw-a, glw-b, and glw-c), all of which carried frameshift mutations predicted to inhibit normal translation of neuropeptide precursor sequences (Figure 3A–D).
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data and analysis shown in Figure 3A–D.

claim: The oral half of the gastrula embryo can develop into a polyp in Nematostella vectensis.
source: Taking advantage of the ability of the oral half of the gastrula embryo to develop into a polyp (cf. [Fritzenwanker et al., 2007; Lee et al., 2007]), a piece of an aboral tissue of each F2 embryo was surgically separated and used for genomic DNA extraction, while the remaining embryo was individually maintained and allowed to regulate and develop into polyps.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Nematostella development, supported by citations.

claim: At 3dpf, glw-b/glw-c null mutants appeared to be morphologically identical to normal swimming planula larvae.
source: At 3dpf, glw-b/glw-c null mutants appeared to be morphologically identical to normal swimming planula larvae (Figure 4A–C,G–I), with an aboral apical tuft (at in Figure 4B,H) and an endoderm in which longitudinal muscle fibers are developing (arrowheads in Figure 4C,I).
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 4A–C,G–I.

claim: By 5dpf, 80% of glw-b/glw-c null mutants had transformed into morphologically normal primary polyps.
source: By 5dpf, the majority of glw-b/glw-c null mutants had transformed into morphologically normal primary polyps (glw-b/glw-c, 80% (n = 35); wildtype control, 78.6% (n = 56); Figure 4D–F,J–L).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data and confocal microscopy shown in Figure 4D–F,J–L.

claim: By 5dpf, 78.6% of wildtype control animals had transformed into morphologically normal primary polyps.
source: By 5dpf, the majority of glw-b/glw-c null mutants had transformed into morphologically normal primary polyps (glw-b/glw-c, 80% (n = 35); wildtype control, 78.6% (n = 56); Figure 4D–F,J–L).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data and confocal microscopy shown in Figure 4D–F,J–L.

claim: glw-b/glw-c null mutants show morphological hallmarks of metamorphosis, including the development of parietal and retractor muscles in the endoderm, the loss of the apical tuft, and the formation of oral tentacles with polyp-specific cell types such as the hair cells.
source: They show morphological hallmarks of metamorphosis, including the development of parietal and retractor muscles in the endoderm (pm and rm in Figure 4D,J), the loss of the apical tuft (arrowheads in Figure 4E,K; [Nakanishi et al., 2012]), and the formation of oral tentacles with polyp-specific cell types such as the hair cells (Figure 4F,L; (Nakanishi et al., 2012; Watson et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 4D–F,J–L and citations.

claim: Other glw null mutants--namely, glw-a/glw-c (F2) and glw-a/glw-a (F3)—also metamorphosed.
source: Other glw null mutants--namely, glw-a/glw-c (F2) and glw-a/glw-a (F3)—also metamorphosed (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from experiments, though data are not shown.

claim: GLWamide of the larval nervous system is dispensable for metamorphosis in N. vectensis.
source: These results demonstrate that GLWamide of the larval nervous system is dispensable for metamorphosis in N. vectensis, and that cnidarian metamorphosis can occur via a GLWamide-independent mechanism.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that null mutants can complete metamorphosis.

claim: Cnidarian metamorphosis can occur via a GLWamide-independent mechanism.
source: These results demonstrate that GLWamide of the larval nervous system is dispensable for metamorphosis in N. vectensis, and that cnidarian metamorphosis can occur via a GLWamide-independent mechanism.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that null mutants can complete metamorphosis.

claim: F2 glw-b/glw-c and wildtype control juvenile polyps can regenerate after being transversely cut into oral and aboral halves.
source: F2 glw-b/glw-c and wildtype control juvenile polyps were transversely cut into oral and aboral halves, which were given two weeks to regenerate the aboral and oral regions, respectively. Regeneration occurred normally in glw-b/glw-c mutants; the oral half regenerated the aboral region (glw-b/glw-c, 100% (n = 6); wildtype control, 83.3% (n = 6), and the aboral half regenerated the oral structures such as the pharynx and oral tentacles (glw-b/glw-c, 100% (n = 6); wildtype control, 100% (n = 6).
evidence: This is supported by regeneration experiments with quantitative data.

claim: GLWamide knockout mutants can generate functional gametes in response to light and temperature cues provided to induce spawning.
source: We also note that although pharmacological evidence suggests a role in oocyte maturation and spawning in a hydrozoan cnidarian (Takeda et al., 2013), GLWamide knockout mutants can generate functional gametes in response to light and temperature cues provided to induce spawning.
evidence: This is an observation from experiments with knockout mutants.

claim: GLWamides are not essential for regeneration or reproduction in N. vectensis.
source: Thus, GLWamides are not essential for regeneration or reproduction in N. vectensis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the regeneration and spawning experiments.

claim: Wildtype control animals began to metamorphose at 6dpf, and the majority (~86%) had begun transforming by 8 dpf.
source: We found that the wildtype control animals began to metamorphose at 6dpf, and the majority (~86%) had begun transforming by 8 dpf, while the null mutants began to metamorphose at 7dpf, and less than half (~42%) had begun metamorphosis by 8 dpf (Figure 5); the differences at 7 and 8 dpf were statistically significant (α = 0.05).
evidence: This is supported by time-course data shown in Figure 5.

claim: GLWamide null mutants began to metamorphose at 7dpf, and less than half (~42%) had begun metamorphosis by 8 dpf.
source: We found that the wildtype control animals began to metamorphose at 6dpf, and the majority (~86%) had begun transforming by 8 dpf, while the null mutants began to metamorphose at 7dpf, and less than half (~42%) had begun metamorphosis by 8 dpf (Figure 5); the differences at 7 and 8 dpf were statistically significant (α = 0.05).
evidence: This is supported by time-course data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The differences in metamorphosis rates between wildtype and null mutants at 7 and 8 dpf were statistically significant (α = 0.05).
source: We found that the wildtype control animals began to metamorphose at 6dpf, and the majority (~86%) had begun transforming by 8 dpf, while the null mutants began to metamorphose at 7dpf, and less than half (~42%) had begun metamorphosis by 8 dpf (Figure 5); the differences at 7 and 8 dpf were statistically significant (α = 0.05).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of time-course data shown in Figure 5.

claim: GLWamide null mutants metamorphosed at a slower rate than the wildtype control.
source: Thus GLWamide null mutants metamorphosed at a slower rate than the wildtype control.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the time-course data.

claim: Null mutants treated with GLWamide began metamorphosis at 6 dpf, and the majority (~84%) had started metamorphosis by 8 dpf.
source: We observed that, similar to the wildtype animals, the null mutants treated with GLWamide began metamorphosis at 6 dpf, and the majority (~84%) had started metamorphosis by 8 dpf, showing statistically higher proportions of metamorphosing animals at 7 and 8 dpf relative to untreated null mutants (α = 0.05; Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Null mutants treated with GLWamide showed statistically higher proportions of metamorphosing animals at 7 and 8 dpf relative to untreated null mutants (α = 0.05).
source: We observed that, similar to the wildtype animals, the null mutants treated with GLWamide began metamorphosis at 6 dpf, and the majority (~84%) had started metamorphosis by 8 dpf, showing statistically higher proportions of metamorphosing animals at 7 and 8 dpf relative to untreated null mutants (α = 0.05; Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of rescue experiment data shown in Figure 5.

claim: GLWamide regulates metamorphosis by accelerating the process in N. vectensis.
source: Taken together, we conclude that GLWamide regulates metamorphosis by accelerating the process in N. vectensis.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the time-course and rescue experiments.

claim: This is the first neuropeptide knockout animals from an early-evolving animal group Cnidaria.
source: Here we created the first neuropeptide knockout animals from an early-evolving animal group Cnidaria, and examined the endogenous function of deeply conserved (GL)Wamide neuropeptides in the sea anemone cnidarian Nematostella vectensis.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the study.

claim: In N. vectensis GLWamide neuropeptides are expressed in ectodermal and endodermal nervous systems of the planula larva.
source: We report that in N. vectensis GLWamide neuropeptides are expressed in ectodermal and endodermal nervous systems of the planula larva, but are not essential for transformation of the planula into a polyp.
evidence: This is supported by expression data presented in the Results section.

claim: GLWamide neuropeptides are not essential for transformation of the planula into a polyp in N. vectensis.
source: We report that in N. vectensis GLWamide neuropeptides are expressed in ectodermal and endodermal nervous systems of the planula larva, but are not essential for transformation of the planula into a polyp.
evidence: This is supported by the observation that null mutants can complete metamorphosis.

claim: GLWamides regulate the timing of polyp formation by accelerating the metamorphic process in N. vectensis.
source: Instead we find that GLWamides regulate the timing of polyp formation by accelerating the metamorphic process in N. vectensis.
evidence: This is supported by time-course data showing delayed metamorphosis in null mutants.

claim: The ancestral role of Wamide neuropeptides in animals may have been to regulate the timing of life cycle transition.
source: These results raise the possibility that the ancestral role of Wamide neuropeptides in animals may have been to regulate the timing of life cycle transition.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about ancestral function based on the current findings.

claim: Exogenous Wamides can trigger life cycle transition across annelids and cnidarians.
source: First, as described above, exogenous Wamides can trigger life cycle transition across annelids and cnidarians (Conzelmann et al., 2013; Erwin and Szmant, 2010; Iwao et al., 2002; Leitz et al., 1994; Schmich et al., 1998b), and our results show slower rates of life cycle transition in GLWamide mutant larvae in sea anemones.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Results show slower rates of life cycle transition in GLWamide mutant larvae in sea anemones.
source: First, as described above, exogenous Wamides can trigger life cycle transition across annelids and cnidarians (Conzelmann et al., 2013; Erwin and Szmant, 2010; Iwao et al., 2002; Leitz et al., 1994; Schmich et al., 1998b), and our results show slower rates of life cycle transition in GLWamide mutant larvae in sea anemones.
evidence: This is supported by the time-course data from the current study.

claim: The data support Wamide's role as an accelerator of metamorphosis across animals.
source: These data support Wamide's role as an accelerator of metamorphosis across animals.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparative evidence across multiple species.

claim: Wamides do not appear necessary for life cycle transition in animals where functional perturbation data are available.
source: Second, Wamides do not appear necessary for life cycle transition in animals where functional perturbation data are available.
evidence: This is an inference based on functional studies cited in the following discussion.

claim: In Platynereis, reducing the expression of MIP by morpholino antisense oligonucleotide inhibits feeding behavior in the juvenile, but not metamorphosis.
source: For instance, although in the annelid polychaete Platynereis, MIP (Wamide) receptor expression is necessary for MIP-induced larval settlement behavior (Conzelmann et al., 2013), reducing the expression of MIP by morpholino antisense oligonucleotide inhibits feeding behavior in the juvenile, but not metamorphosis (Williams et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: In Hydractinia echinata, in one of the three experimental conditions where RNAi was used to knockdown GLWamide expression, the rate of metamorphosis was significantly reduced at 24 hr after induction, but it increased to a normal level 24 hr later.
source: In the hydrozoan cnidarian Hydractinia echinata it is noteworthy that in one of the three experimental conditions where RNAi was used to knockdown GLWamide expression, the rate of metamorphosis was significantly reduced at 24 hr after induction (by CsCl), but it increased to a normal level 24 hr later (Plickert et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: This observation is consistent with a role of GLWamide as an accelerator, but not an essential regulator, of metamorphosis.
source: This observation is consistent with a role of GLWamide as an accelerator, but not an essential regulator, of metamorphosis; however, an alternative possiblity that GLWamide expression recovered at later stages (due to reagent degradation and/or dilution) cannot be ruled out without gene knockout data.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited observation.

claim: Gene knockout data clearly demonstrate that GLWamides are not required for life cycle transition in the sea anemone cnidarian N. vectensis.
source: In the present study, our gene knockout data clearly demonstrate that GLWamides are not required for life cycle transition in the sea anemone cnidarian N. vectensis.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data from the current study.

claim: Other amidated peptides could be necessary for metamorphosis in N. vectensis.
source: We note that our data leave open the possibility that other amidated peptides could be necessary for metamorphosis in N. vectensis.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about alternative mechanisms.

claim: Deuterostome bilaterians lack Wamide homologs despite metamorphosis being common in some of the lineages.
source: For example, deuterostome bilaterians lack Wamide homologs (Conzelmann et al., 2013) despite metamorphosis being common in some of the lineages (e.g. echinoderms, hemichordates, ascidians, and vertebrates).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and general knowledge of deuterostome biology.

claim: Members of Porifera (sponges) typically undergo metamorphosis, and yet Wamides have not been found in a sponge genome.
source: Similarly, members of Porifera (sponges)—an outgroup to Eumetazoa—typically undergo metamorphosis, and yet Wamides have not been found in a sponge genome (Srivastava et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to genomic data.

claim: Wamide-independent mechanisms of metamorphosis must exist in some animal lineages.
source: Thus Wamide-independent mechanisms of metamorphosis must exist in some animal lineages.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that some animals undergo metamorphosis without Wamides.

claim: The ancestral Wamide neuropeptidergic signaling was not an indispensable component of the developmental regulatory system, but may have functioned to fine-tune the timing of life cycle transition by accelerating the developmental process in the last common ancestor of Eumetazoa.
source: Taken together, comparative evidence suggests that the ancestral Wamide neuropeptidergic signaling was not an indispensable component of the developmental regulatory system, but may have functioned to fine-tune the timing of life cycle transition by accelerating the developmental process—possibly in response to specific environmental cues—in the last common ancestor of Eumetazoa.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about ancestral function based on comparative evidence.

claim: Treatment with MIPs can suppress spontaneous contractions of the hindgut in insects.
source: For instance, treatment with MIPs can suppress spontaneous contractions of the hindgut in insects (Schoofs et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: In the annelid Platynereis, MIPs increase gut peristalsis and are necessary for feeding behavior.
source: In the annelid Platynereis, in contrast, MIPs increase gut peristalsis and are necessary for feeding behavior (Williams et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Exogenous GLWamides can induce muscle contractions in hydrozoan and anthozoan polyps.
source: In cnidarians, exogenous GLWamides can induce muscle contractions in hydrozoan and anthozoan polyps (Takahashi et al., 2003) and stimulate migration of planula larvae in Hydractinia (Katsukura et al., 2004); however, it remains to be confirmed whether GLWamides endogenously control these behavioral processes.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Exogenous GLWamides can stimulate migration of planula larvae in Hydractinia.
source: In cnidarians, exogenous GLWamides can induce muscle contractions in hydrozoan and anthozoan polyps (Takahashi et al., 2003) and stimulate migration of planula larvae in Hydractinia (Katsukura et al., 2004); however, it remains to be confirmed whether GLWamides endogenously control these behavioral processes.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: It remains to be confirmed whether GLWamides endogenously control muscle contractions and larval migration in cnidarians.
source: In cnidarians, exogenous GLWamides can induce muscle contractions in hydrozoan and anthozoan polyps (Takahashi et al., 2003) and stimulate migration of planula larvae in Hydractinia (Katsukura et al., 2004); however, it remains to be confirmed whether GLWamides endogenously control these behavioral processes.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of current knowledge.

claim: The anti-GLWamide antibody used in this study can cross-react with GLWamides with divergent N-terminal sequences.
source: This immunostaining pattern is consistent with that previously documented by using an antibody against EQPGLWamide (Nakanishi et al., 2009), indicating that the anti-GLWamide antibody used in this study can cross-react with GLWamides with divergent N-terminal sequences.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of staining patterns in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 with prior research.

claim: F3 null mutants lack GLWamide immunostaining.
source: Note the lack of GLWamide immunostaining in glw-/glw- null mutants, which provides experimental evidence that there are no other GLWamide-like peptides present at the developmental stages investigated.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: There are no other GLWamide-like peptides present at the developmental stages investigated in N. vectensis.
source: Note the lack of GLWamide immunostaining in glw-/glw- null mutants, which provides experimental evidence that there are no other GLWamide-like peptides present at the developmental stages investigated.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the lack of immunostaining in null mutants shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: NvLWamide-like does not generate GLWamides.
source: Thus NvLWamide-like does not generate GLWamides, as predicted from the amino acid sequence data (see main text).
evidence: This is supported by the lack of immunostaining in null mutants (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) and sequence analysis.
